newsitem.title: UK: Britain admits nuclear dumping in Irish Sea.
newsitem.headline: Britain admits nuclear dumping in Irish Sea.

text.p: After years of vehement denials, Britain was forced to admit on Monday it had secretly dumped radioactive waste in the Irish Sea in the 1950s.

The Scottish Office confirmed a report in the Guardian newspaper that said up to two tonnes of low-level nuclear waste, packed in heavy metal drums and encased in concrete, had been dropped in the ocean betwen Scotland and Northern Ireland.

"Ministers have recently been made aware that small quantities of low- to intermediate-contaminated waste were dumped in the 1950s. Prior to the discovery, ministers were not aware it had been dumped," a Scottish Office spokesman said.

Ireland's Minister for the Marine and Natural Resources, David Woods, expressed "deep concern" at the news. "Firm assurances had been given in the past that no radioactive material had been dumped," Woods said in a statement.

Woods said he was demanding full information from the London government and would be taking up the matter with British officials immediately. British officials said the dumping only came to light recently in government papers from the 1950s found in the Public Record Office.

Britain has consistently denied persistent reports of nuclear waste dumping in the Beaufort's Dyke area, which is close to three ferry routes and a gas pipeline being built between Scotland and British-ruled Northern Ireland.
Beaufort Dyke is a sea channel about six miles off the Scottish coast used as a munitions dump from 1945 until 1976.

Successive Irish governments have voiced concern at British policy on nuclear waste and on the location of a nuclear reprocessing plant at Sellafield on the Cumbrian coast, in the far north of England.

The Guardian said the waste was mostly from civilian sources, such as laboratories. The spokesman said details of the materials and quantities that were dumped are still being investigated and that Britain's new Labour government would make a full statement shortly.
But he said the levels of radioactive material were so insignificant that they could not be measured. The Conservative Party was in power from 1979 to May 1 this year.
Scottish National Party member of parliament, Alasdair Morgan, called for a public inquiry into why the government had denied dumping for so long.

"If it is because they did not know, then that raises huge concerns over the secretive nature of this activity, and a question mark over what else may be dumped there, or indeed elsewhere in Scotland," he said.

"Yet despite the many safety, environmental and economic considerations at stake, successive British governments have behaved in an appalling and irresponsible fashion - and then indulged in secrecy and cover-up in order to mask their folly."

Hundreds of bombs, bullets, flares and grenades have been washed ashore along the coasts of Scotland, Northern Ireland and England and the Isle of Man, and trawled up by small fishing boats following the use of Beaufort's Dyke as a munitions dumping ground.
Nerve gas and chemical warfare agents were also dumped in the north Atlantic, according to media reports.
